data.name: Hugz

audit.sub: Where the account is leaking and where the upside is. All figures are Klaviyo-attributed unless noted; windows are the last 12 complete months through July 2026. This audit covers campaigns and the automation layer, since the two compound together.

wins.title: Send more campaigns, all year (biggest single opportunity)
wins.detail: Hold 12 to 16 sends a month year-round, built on the concepts that already work.

wins.title: Build the missing retention flows
wins.detail: Win-back, replenishment, VIP and a birthday engine, plus the new Evergreen flow.

wins.title: Turn single-send launches into launch sequences
wins.detail: Teaser, launch and last-chance on each drop that already works as one email.

wins.title: Deepen the half-built flows
wins.detail: Most flows are a single email; extend the ones carrying real revenue.

wins.title: Turn opens into clicks
wins.detail: Opens are strong; the leak is the click, so rebuild for one clear action.

wins.title: Win back the dormant list
wins.detail: A separate win-back sequence to the ~83k dormant profiles before they are cleaned.

wins.title: Start a real testing program
wins.detail: Only 2 of 8 flows have ever been tested; a steady test cadence compounds on every fix above.

wins.title: Tighten abandonment re-entry (and add an IDR layer)
wins.detail: Re-open abandonment in 4 to 7 days, not 14 to 30, and add identity resolution (Aimerce) so the flows reach more anonymous abandoners.

audit.title: Account audit

todos.name: Hugz: Send more campaigns year-round
todos.notes: Hold 12 to 16 sends a month all year on the concepts that already work. Non-BFCM cadence rose from ~2 to ~6/mo with revenue tracking it, and it has not hit a ceiling. Biggest single lever (~$260k/yr).

todos.name: Hugz: Build the missing retention flows
todos.notes: No win-back, replenishment, VIP or birthday flows, and no evergreen flow built from top past campaigns. Build these out; the evergreen tends to jump into the top flows on launch (~$180k/yr).

todos.name: Hugz: Add a cart abandonment flow
todos.notes: You run checkout, browse and site abandonment but no added-to-cart flow, which is the highest-intent abandoner and usually the biggest of the set. A cart flow already sits in the GBE drafts, so it is a tested switch-on away.

todos.name: Hugz: Turn launches into email sequences
todos.notes: Named-character launches and restocks are your top campaigns but each goes out as a single email. Build each into a teaser, launch, last-chance arc (~$100k/yr).

todos.name: Hugz: Deepen the half-built flows
todos.notes: Most flows are a single email. Extend the ones carrying real revenue so there are more chances to open and buy (~$90k/yr).

todos.name: Hugz: Rebuild campaigns for the click
todos.notes: Opens look strong (Apple-inflated) but the click lags at ~2.6%. Rebuild layout, offer and CTA around one clear action, and lead on revenue per recipient, not open rate (~$45k/yr).

todos.name: Hugz: Tighten abandonment re-entry
todos.notes: Checkout re-opens after 14 days, browse and site after 30. Reset to about 4 to 7 days so repeat abandoners are not locked out. Fast and low risk.

todos.name: Hugz: Add an IDR layer (Aimerce)
todos.notes: Most abandonment traffic is anonymous, so the flows only reach already-identified visitors. Add identity resolution (recommended Aimerce) so the abandonment flows reach far more of the people abandoning.

todos.name: Hugz: Win back the dormant list
todos.notes: About 83k of the 120k master list are dormant. Run a separate win-back sequence, kept off the core for deliverability, before they are cleaned (~$35k/yr).

todos.name: Hugz: Start an A/B testing program
todos.notes: Only 2 of 8 flows have ever been tested and none run now. Stand up a steady test cadence so every fix compounds.

todos.name: Hugz: Test the 15% cashback offer
todos.notes: The popup offers Fondue cashback instead of an upfront discount. Repeat rate is ~6% (1.06 orders/buyer) and Fondue is not tracked in Klaviyo. A/B a straight first-order discount vs cashback, measure first-order conversion AND repeat, and pipe Fondue events into Klaviyo.

todos.name: Hugz: Resolve the pending flow conflict
todos.notes: 8 live EG flows vs 10 staged GBE draft flows. Do not hard-swap: deepen first, then test the new creative against the live control message by message and only promote what beats it.

todos.name: Hugz: Build the SMS list, then test
todos.notes: SMS runs at a low trickle with zero new subscribers captured all year. Collect SMS consent at popup and checkout, build the list, then run a holdout to prove it lifts revenue before scaling spend.

todos.name: Hugz: A/B test the popup offer
todos.notes: The popup is clean and on-brand but the single offer is never tested. A/B the offer (cashback vs instant discount vs free shipping) and watch the not-valid-with-a-coupon rule.

findings.body: The store did about $3.93M over the last 12 months and is growing fast, up roughly 99% year on year, at an $84 average order value. Email and SMS are credited with $687k, about 17.5%. Email grew about 90% over the same window, so the program is scaling with the store but has not pulled ahead. A well-run program on a store this size sits between 25% and 35%. Closing to 25% is worth roughly $295k a year, to 30% closer to $490k. Our longest-managed client, on the same playbook, floats between 35% and 38%, so on a store this size there is room well beyond 30% here.
findings.title: Email and SMS drive 17.5% of a $3.9M store

findings.body: About 73 campaigns went out last year, four to six a month most of the year, ramping to nine to eleven in November and December. Here is the proof it scales: non-holiday sends rose from about two a month in 2023 to nearly six in 2026, and campaign revenue moved with them, from roughly $1k a month to $24k, a 0.79 correlation. Your best non-holiday month, May 2026 at nine sends, earned $46k. Cadence has not hit a ceiling. Holding twelve to sixteen a month year-round is the fastest six-figure lever.

chart.ideasSub: Four to six suggested sends a month, built from the angles that have worked best in this account. Revenue per send is estimated conservatively from your last 12 months: an average send earns about $3.9k at the current list size, with standout concepts and multi-email arcs (launch teaser, launch, last-chance) earning more. No discounting assumed.

findings.title: Campaigns go out about six times a month, and you have proven more works

findings.body:
People are opening, though open rate is a soft metric these days: Apple Mail Privacy auto-opens inflate it, so we do not lean on it as a measure of real engagement.

The click is where it thins out, which points at the offer, layout and call to action rather than the subject line. That is good news: content and testing work on traffic you already reach, so lifting the click converts cheaply. It is also why we lead on revenue per recipient and orders, not open rate.

chart.leak: Opens read high but are inflated by Apple Mail Privacy, so the click is the honest read, and that gap is the opportunity.

findings.title: Strong opens, but the clicks lag

findings.body: Seven flows are live. The Welcome series carries the account. After that, several are single-message stubs. Back In Stock earns $5.94 an email on one message, excellent and badly underbuilt. Repeat Order Nurture sends 73,000 emails for $12k, about 17 cents an email, so it is mistargeted or doing a job win-back and replenishment should own.
findings.title: Every flow at a glance

findings.body:
The one glaring gap on the abandonment side is cart abandonment. You run checkout, browse and site abandonment, but there is no added-to-cart flow, and added-to-cart is the highest-intent abandoner and usually the single biggest money-maker of the set. A cart flow already exists in the draft package, so it is one tested switch-on away.

Beyond that, the retention side, the part that makes a fast-growing store durable, is largely missing: no win-back, no replenishment, no VIP track, no birthday engine, and no evergreen flow built from your best past campaigns (that one tends to jump straight into the top flows once live). On a $3.9M store this is a six-figure layer.

chart.note: Live means the flow exists and is sending. Missing means there is no automation covering it today.
missing: Cart abandonment (added-to-cart — highest intent, usually the biggest of the set)
Evergreen (best-of past campaigns, lands in the top flows fast)

findings.title: The retention layer is half-built

findings.body:
The account holds two full flow sets. Eight live flows built by your current email agency (the EG set) are running now. Sitting alongside them are ten draft flows from a second provider (the GBE set): a redesigned package covering the welcome series, the abandonment flows, and post-purchase, staged and waiting to be switched on.

The usual next move is to flip the new package live and turn the old flows off in one go. The problem is there is no test in that. Redesigned emails almost always look nicer, so they get shipped and the old ones get killed, and for months nobody actually knows whether performance went up, stayed flat, or quietly dropped. In practice the wins and losses tend to cancel out: message one does a little better, message two a little worse, and you are left with prettier emails and roughly the same revenue, sometimes a little less.

That is the real risk of a hard swap. You can burn months, and at worst dent an account that was working, with no data to show what happened.

We work the other way around. First we deepen the flows that already earn, so there are more chances to open and buy. Then we test the new creative against what is live, message by message, and only promote what genuinely beats the control. We never hard-update a working account on the assumption that the prettier version wins, because after enough testing you learn how often it does not.

chart.note: Eight live flows are running; ten redesigned drafts are staged to switch on. Flipping the new set live and turning the current one off in a single move is a hard swap with no test behind it, so there is no way to know if it helped or hurt.

items.label: Live flows now (your current agency, EG)
Draft flows staged to replace them (GBE)

findings.title: Two competing flow sets, with a redesign staged to hard-swap the live one

findings.body:
Two settings decide whether an abandoner actually gets the flow: how fast the first message fires, and how long before the same person is allowed back in. The first-message timing here is fine, 15 minutes to 2 hours. The re-entry window is the problem. Checkout re-opens after 14 days, and browse and site after 30. Someone who abandons twice in the same month only ever gets the flow once.

Abandonment should re-open in about 4 to 7 days. Tightening the re-entry window is a fast, low-risk change that recovers the repeat abandoners you are currently locking out, and it costs nothing to ship.

There is a bigger lever alongside it. Most abandonment traffic is anonymous, so these flows can only reach the small slice of visitors already identified in Klaviyo. An identity-resolution layer, we would recommend Aimerce, matches far more anonymous sessions to a contactable profile, so the abandonment flows can actually fire for a much larger share of the people abandoning. Paired with a tighter re-entry window, the same flows suddenly reach a far bigger audience without building anything new.
findings.title: Abandonment flows re-open too slowly, so repeat abandoners miss them

findings.body: The welcome series earns about $210k, roughly 52% of all flow revenue. It is a strong flow, but resting the automation layer on one flow is a concentration risk. The fix is the same as the retention gaps above: build the missing flows so revenue sits on a wider base.

chart.note: One flow carries the automation layer. If the welcome series dips, most automated revenue dips with it. Building the other flows spreads both the risk and the upside.

findings.title: Half of flow revenue rides on one flow

findings.body: The winning concept is clear. Named-character launches and restocks are the top ten campaigns of the year, from Unicorn and Midnight the Bat to the Maybelline collaboration, each $6k to $11k. But they run as one email apiece. The demand is proven; the touches are missing.

chart.note: Launch and restock sends earn 77% more than everything else, and each goes out as a single email. Building each drop into a teaser, launch, and last-chance arc is the clearest way to scale a concept that already works.

findings.title: Launches win, but each is a single email

findings.body:
About 10,500 SMS went out over the year, so SMS is not off, it is just a thin, steady trickle rather than a real channel. And not one new SMS subscriber was captured in 12 months, so the list behind it is not even growing.

On a US gifting store SMS could be a genuine add or a money pit, and we would not pour budget in blind. The move is to start collecting SMS consent at the popup and checkout, build the list, then run a proper holdout to prove SMS lifts revenue before scaling spend.

chart.note: Email vs SMS revenue per month. SMS is the thin gold cap: it ticks along at a low, steady level (about 8.6% of attributed revenue) rather than being actively pushed, and no new SMS subscribers were collected all year. Before scaling spend, build the list and run a holdout to prove it lifts revenue.

findings.title: SMS is running, but nowhere near full strength

findings.body: We checked. Across the eight live flows there are two completed A/B tests and nothing running now, and campaigns are rarely tested, so the lifecycle is not learning. Every send is a chance to test a subject line, an offer, or a layout, and small consistent wins compound. This is cheap upside on traffic you already have.

chart.themSub: flows with a completed A/B test, none running now; campaigns rarely tested

findings.title: Testing has barely started

findings.body: November and December run about $720k each against roughly $210k in the quiet months and a January trough near $165k. This is a gifting business, so the shape is structural. The off-season is the place to test and to build the retention layer, and a birthday and loved-ones gifting engine seeds demand year-round rather than only at the holidays.
findings.title: A strong Q4 peak and a deep off-season

findings.body: Credit where it is due. The four-message welcome series earned about $210k across 2,215 orders. It is well-built and doing real work. The opportunity is to bring that same craft to the flows that are one message or missing entirely.

chart.note: The welcome series alone earns more than the next two flows combined. It is the model to extend across the rest of the automation layer.

findings.title: The welcome series is genuinely strong

findings.body: We do the unglamorous work: the calendar, the flows, the testing, compounding into a retention system that does not falter. We work with stores from $3M to $20M, most between $5M and $8M. If the numbers above look like money left on the table, let's talk.
findings.title: Where Zee.Media comes in

findings.body: Capture volume is healthy: roughly 4,600 new email opt-ins and 1,000 new SMS opt-ins a month, so the top of the funnel is working. The popup itself is well built. It is on-brand, the two-step email then SMS flow is best practice, and the SMS consent language is compliant. The open question is the offer. It is a single static 15% cashback that, as far as we can see, never gets tested, and cashback (store credit redeemed later) tends to convert first-time buyers differently than an instant discount. That, plus the quiet “not valid if a coupon is applied” rule, is exactly the kind of thing worth A/B testing rather than leaving fixed.

chart.note: The current three-step mobile popup. Clean and on-brand; the lever is the offer, not the design.

callouts.text: On-brand and uncluttered, with a clear single field at each step.
Two-step email then SMS is best practice, and the SMS consent copy is compliant.
One offer, never tested: a static 15% cashback leaves signups and first orders on the table.
A/B the offer: 15% cashback vs an instant 10 to 15% off vs free shipping. Cashback protects margin but can convert first orders worse, so prove it.
Watch the “not valid with a coupon” rule: it quietly excludes deal-seekers, so track it against redemption.

chart.note: Average new opt-ins a month over the last 12 months, by channel. Capture volume is strong on both.

findings.title: The popup is clean and on-brand; the offer is a single untested lever

findings.body:
The popup offer runs on Fondue. Instead of an upfront discount, the shopper is promised 15% back after they buy, redeemed later as store credit or a prepaid card through a post-purchase email. Redemption is not guaranteed, which is how Fondue protects margin. The popup converts at about 3.6%.

The trade-off is on the first order. A first-time visitor who expects a discount does not get one, so the pull to place that first order is weaker, which tends to lower first-order conversion and push acquisition costs up. The reward only lands on a second purchase, and a lot of buyers never make one.

The data backs the concern. Over the last 12 months 44,119 people bought, placing 46,725 orders between them, about 1.06 each. At most around 6% came back for a second order. The whole point of cashback is to drive that second purchase, and the second purchase is barely happening.

It is also invisible. Fondue sends and redemptions are not tracked as events in Klaviyo, so right now there is no way to see how many people redeem, or whether the cashback changes behaviour at all.

Cashback is not wrong, it should just be earned in a test rather than assumed. We would run a straight first-order discount against the cashback and measure both first-order conversion and the repeat rate, and pipe Fondue events into Klaviyo so the second-order effect is finally measurable.

chart.note: Over the last 12 months 44,119 people bought, but only about 2,600 (~6%) placed a second order, roughly 1.06 orders per buyer. Cashback is meant to drive that second order; it is not landing, and Fondue is not tracked in Klaviyo so it cannot be measured.

findings.title: The 15% cashback offer may be costing you first orders and repeats

findings.body: The master list holds about 120,000 profiles, but you concentrate sends on the roughly 37,000 recently active profiles, and a typical campaign reaches about 34,000. That is good practice: mailing the engaged core protects deliverability and keeps the whole program healthy. The flip side is a dormant tail of roughly 83,000 profiles that rarely hear from you. A dedicated win-back sequence, kept separate from the core so it cannot hurt deliverability, is the way to test whether any of that tail is still reachable before it is cleaned.

chart.note: You mail the active core, which is correct. The gap between the master list and the active core, about 83,000 profiles, is the win-back opportunity.
chart.freqHead: Reach narrows to the engaged core by design

findings.title: You mail the engaged core well; a large dormant tail is the win-back
